      <title>Saudi-Arabia: Har skutt ned houthi-missiler</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/saudi-arabia_-har-skutt-ned-houthi-missiler-1.18086194</link>
      <description>Tre missiler som hadde retning mot Saudi-Arabias hovedstad Riyadh er skutt ned.
Det sier den saudiledede militærkoalisjonen, som en i pågående væpnet konflikt med houthi-militsen.
I tillegg skal det vært hørt flere eksplosjoner i Riyadh, melder Reuters.
Saudi-Arabia gikk til krig mot houthi-militsen i Jemen i 2015. Etter sju år med krig avtalte partene en våpenhvile i 2022.
I sommer har konflikten blusset opp igjen.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/historisk-_gta-6_-lansering_-solgte-for-nesten-4-milliarder-dollar-pa-en-dag-1.18086187</link>
      <description>Spillgiganten Rockstar Games knuser alle rekorder, melder Variety.
Allerede på lanseringsdagen omsatte «Grand Theft Auto 6», også kjent som «GTA 6», for 3,79 milliarder dollar.
Det tilsvarer over 37 milliarder norske kroner, og spillet forbigår dermed superheltfilmen «Avengers: End Game» som den største underholdningslanseringen noensinne.
«GTA 6» ble lansert torsdag på PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X og S, i tillegg til at det kan strømmes på Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming.
I den sjette utgaven av actionspillet følger spillerne duoen Jason og Lucia mens de ufører ran og andre kriminelle oppdrag i den fiktive amerikanske delstaten Leonida.</description>

      <description>Norwegian har teke kontakt med rundt 5000 kundar og bede dei sperre bankkorta sine etter at ein leverandør til nettsidene deira er utsett for datainnbrot, melder NTB.

    <item>
      <title>Israel med ny offensiv – tre drept</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/israel-med-ny-offensiv-_-tre-drept-1.18084431</link>
      <description>Israels hær sier den har innledet en operasjon i Hamas-kontrollerte områder i Gaza
Israel har innledet en militæroperasjon i det sentrale Gaza vest for den såkalte gule linjen, som har skilt Hamas-kontrollerte og israelsk-kontrollerte områder siden våpenhvilen trådte i kraft i fjor. Det opplyser militæret til AFP.
Vitner sier at israelske stridsvogner rullet inn på hovedveien Salahudeen, vest for den såkalte gule linjen som markerer grensen for de to tredjedelene av Gazastripen som fortsatt er under israelsk kontroll.
Den såkalte gule linjen ble etablert etter våpenhvilen i oktober 2025 og skiller israelskkontrollerte og palestinske soner i Gazastripen. Israelske styrker har gradvis flyttet den gule linjen og utvidet området under direkte militær kontroll i Gaza.</description>

Gatherings are taking place across Canada Friday for Transgender Day of Remembrance, including a rally in the capital, just hours after the swearing-in of new Premier Lorne Doerkson and his B.C. Conservative cabinet, prompting concerns from advocacy groups about policy shifts.

In Victoria, groups were scheduled to meet outside the B.C. Legislature at 4 p.m. to recognize ongoing violence and elevated risks facing transgender, nonbinary, Two-Spirit, and gender diverse and gender-variant people whose lives have been lost due to transgender violence.

Statistics Canada finds transgender and non-binary populations face a disproportionately higher risk of violence compared to cisgender men and women.

In 2025, 148 women and girls were killed by violence, according to a study by Women and Gender Equality Canada.

On Sept. 28, 2026, Doerkson said, “I firmly believe that we have to repeal SOGI”. Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity is anti-bullying curriculum introduced by the former B.C. NDP government in 2016-2017. Doerkson said it had become a source of division in the province, while stating schools must remain safe for children. 

The Public Service Alliance of Canada criticized the pledge to remove SOGI 123 resources, citing a B.C. member survey where half of trans and gender-diverse respondents reported workplace discrimination, harassment, or racism. 

In 2017, the former B.C. NDP Government noted studies showing SOGI policies improve school climates and reduce discrimination and suicide attempts for all students.

On Friday, the BC Greens expressed disappointment over Caroline Elliott’s appointment as Attorney General on Transgender Day of Remembrance, citing Elliot’s past suggestion to use the Notwithstanding Clause regarding trans rights and raising concerns for Indigenous and provincial human rights.

Gender-based violence in Canada

In the past year, gender diverse people were nearly four times as likely as cisgender people to experience violence—76 per cent compared to 32 per cent over the past year, according to Statistics Canada.

In response to this, Federal Minister Rechie Valdez said Friday, “These numbers are a stark reminder of the barriers too many Canadians continue to face simply for being who they are.” 

Valedz, minister of women and gender equality and secretary of state for small business and tourism, pointed to the ministry’s plans to support safer spaces for gender diverse people through its proposed 2026 federal budget.

The ministry plans to fund 2SLGBTQI+ community projects with $60 million over four years and $15 million each year after.

In Canada, transgender and non-binary people experience higher rates of physical and sexual assault than cisgender people:

  • Physical assault: Affected 13% of transgender men, 12% of non-binary people, and 8.7% of transgender women, compared to 3.6% of cisgender men and 2.5% of cisgender women.
  • Sexual assault: Affected 7% of non-binary people, 6.3% of transgender women, and 5.9% of transgender men, compared to 2.3% of cisgender women and 0.8% of cisgender men.

Unwanted online behaviour targeted three times as many gender-diverse individuals as cisgender people in 2025, a heightened risk that persists across all age groups according to StatsCan. 

And the range of online violence—such as harassment, cyberstalking, and non-consensual sharing of explicit material—was linked to higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation and attempts among 2SLGBTQ+ people.

Advocacy groups are working to create safer spaces to protect gender diverse populations 

Advocacy groups remain cautious as the new provincial government takes office.

In November 2026, a B.C. Human Rights Tribunal ruling highlights current workplace discrimination in B.C. The tribunal ordered LifeLabs and its subsidiary, Excelleris Technologies, to pay $32,000 for injury to dignity—plus lost wages and expert report costs—over incidents involving three transgender and non-binary Lower Mainland patients that caused them to avoid medical care in 2019.

A 2025 Journal of Adolescent Health study finds that parent and caregiver acceptance lowers suicide attempt risk for LGBTQ+ youth, highlighting the need for culturally competent support and policies across diverse families. 

In addition to the rally, UVSS Pride and the Gender Empowerment Centre points to online resources and urges people to support gender-diverse peers by speaking against hateful speech, respecting pronouns, staying informed through trans media, advocating for medical care, housing and hiring trans people, and opposing discriminatory legislation. 

The rally for Trans Day of Remembrance takes place from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. at the BC Legislature.

CHEK requested comment from the provincial government but did not receive a response.

Unifor Local 333, the union representing hundreds of BC Transit workers, says it will hold a one-day, system-wide strike in Greater Victoria on Nov. 27.

The strike comes after more than a year of negotiations with BC Transit, with the union’s last contract expiring more than 19 months ago.

The union says it has offered to go to mediation and use an independent arbitrator to settle the labour dispute, but that BC Transit has declined.

“Transit workers in Victoria have done everything they can to reach a fair deal, including offering to let an independent arbitrator settle the outstanding issues. BC Transit keeps saying no,” said Unifor national president Lana Payne in a release Friday. 

“Our members promised riders ample notice and they are keeping that promise. BC Transit has one week to get serious about a fair agreement,” she said.

On Nov. 16, BC Transit said rolling strikes could start as early as Nov. 17. Some labour action, like an overtime ban, had been in place since Oct. 5.

When cancellations started occurring on Nov. 17, Unifor Local 333 said the cancellations were due to the overtime ban, and not because of strike action.

The union said at the time that BC Transit caused unnecessary anxiety by announcing that strike action would potentially begin. Instead, the union said it promised it would give riders more of a warning before job action began.

“BC Transit has shown its true colours twice this week. First, it caused widespread anxiety among riders with a false strike announcement. Now, it is doubling down on making riders and frontline workers do more with less,” said Unifor Local 333-BC president Stephen Bains. 

“When the buses stop on Friday, November 27, we hope BC Transit remembers who keeps them moving and why we keep them moving.”

Unifor Local 333-BC  represents nearly 800 workers, including transit operators and mechanics at BC Transit in Greater Victoria.

The union’s collective agreement expired on March 31, 2025 and job action has been escalating since August.

“Nobody wants the buses to stop, least of all the operators and mechanics who keep this system running,” said Unifor Western regional director Gavin McGarrigle. “The union put savings on the table and offered binding arbitration to settle this. BC Transit and the provincial government still have time to find the funding and the will to reach a fair deal.”

CHEK News has reached out to BC Transit for comment.

]]>

Parks Canada says military support for avalanche control along a major highway corridor in southeastern British Columbia will continue, at least for now, in an apparent reversal of a decision to end the program next year.

Artillery shells have been fired to set off slides along the Trans-Canada Highway, which winds through Rogers Pass in Glacier National Park, for more than 60 years.

B.C’s Transportation Ministry expressed concern earlier this year when the Department of National Defence announced the latest five-year agreement with Parks Canada would not be renewed after its expiry in 2027.

The department cited modernization policies and divestment of what it called legacy artillery systems. 

But after further consideration, Parks Canada says “there is currently no set end date” for the operation, which involves gun crews who fire 105-millimetre howitzer field guns to bring down snow to prevent unplanned avalanches.

A statement from Parks Canada says it’s working with the Canadian Armed Forces to develop a transition plan for the future of avalanche control in the area and the military will continue its involvement in the meantime.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

British Columbia’s police watchdog is investigating the case of a driver who was injured when her truck crashed into a concrete barrier while fleeing police.

The Independent Investigations Office says it happened near Chetwynd in northeastern B.C. on Nov. 8, when an RCMP officer spotted three pickup trucks speeding on Highway 29 near Jackfish Lake Road.

Police tried to stop the trucks, and while two obeyed the command, the third kept driving.

The watchdog says the same driver failed to stop again for another officer and the truck later crashed into a concrete barrier near Boucher Lake Road.

The office says the woman who was driving did not originally appear to have sustained serious injuries, though she complained of pain and she was taken to hospital, while a man in the passenger seat was not seriously injured.

Mounties didn’t call the watchdog at the time because the woman’s injuries didn’t appear to meet the threshold for serious harm, but police have since learned she was transferred to another hospital with injuries more serious than initially thought.

The watchdog investigates incidents involving police officers that result in serious harm or death to determine if there is a link to police action or inaction. 

The office is asking any witnesses or anyone with information on the crash to call its witness line or fill out a contact form on its website. 

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

Central Saanich Police say a suspect was arrested Thursday afternoon following a “serious assault” that sent a person to hospital with a significant injury.

Police say they received multiple 911 calls about a woman wielding an “edged weapon” at approximately 1:30 p.m. near the intersection of Lochside Drive and Hackett Crescent. 

By the time police arrived, the suspect had already fled in a vehicle, but at the scene officers found a person suffering from a “serious, potentially life-threatening injury to their arm.”

Officers provided emergency first aid to the person until they were taken to hospital.

Meanwhile, a large-scale search was launched for the suspect, including help from Saanich Police, Sidney/North Saanich RCMP, Greater Victoria Emergency Response Team, and E-Comm.

The suspect was eventually located and arrested in Saanich, then brought to Central Saanich Police headquarters to be held in custody.

“This investigation remains ongoing. No further information is being released at this time,” said Central Saanich Police in a release Friday.

Anyone with information on the incident or who may have dashcam footage of the area is asked to email Central Saanich Police at tips@cspolice.ca.

“Our officers responded quickly to a very serious and dynamic incident,” said Central Saanich Police Chief Ian Lawson. “Their immediate priority was the injured person, providing critical first aid while other resources worked together to locate and arrest the suspect.”

“I’m extremely proud of their response and grateful for the support of our regional policing partners and E-Comm. This is an excellent example of agencies working together to keep our communities safe,” he said.

Correction: A previous version of this story said the assault happened at 1:30 a.m. In fact, it ocurred at 1:30 p.m.

The CRD says the sightings may be related to other recent sightings of a cougar at Bear Hill Regional Park. Signs have been set up at both parks warning of the sightings, but no trail closures have been recommended, says the CRD in consultation with the BC Conservation Officer Service.

“Although there was no aggressive or abnormal behavior reported during this morning’s sighting, the CRD reminds park visitors that we do share our natural areas with all types of large carnivores,” said the regional district Friday.

“Always stay alert and use caution and watch for signs of wildlife nearby, such as tracks, claw marks on trees and scat.”

Visitors are also reminded to keep their pets on leash at all times to reduce the risk of surprise encounters with predators, and to never feed or approach wildlife.

If you do run into a cougar, WildSafeBC recommends that you keep calm and never run, pick up children and small pets immediately, and make yourself look as large as possible while backing away slowly.

People should keep the cougar in view and give it a clear exit to leave. If you are attacked, you should fight back by focusing on the cougar’s face and eyes with anything on hand, such as rocks, sticks, personal belongings or bear spray.

Anyone concerned about their safety due to wildlife is asked to call the BC Conservation Officer Service RAPP line at 1-877-952-7277, says the CRD.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Canada is feeling “emboldened” but his administration is working on a trade deal “that’s fair” in a wide-ranging news conference at the White House on Friday.

The president said he spoke with Prime Minister Mark Carney on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific economic summit in Shenzhen, China, and described the Canadian leader as “very nice.”

Trump then turned to his repeated claims about Canada ripping off the United States and being frustrating to deal with on the trade file.

“For some reason they feel emboldened and we can’t let them feel that way anymore,” Trump said.

It wasn’t clear exactly what the president was referring to — the historically close Canada-U.S. relationship or the midterm elections which saw American voters issue a clear rebuke of Trump’s trade policy and sweeping tariff campaign.

Trump’s trade war with Canada rapidly escalated after negotiations broke down in August. The president hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs and banned imports of others.

Trump also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and spent days posting images on social media disparaging Canada.

The Trump administration’s tone on Canada softened somewhat after the Republican wipeout in the midterm elections.

On Nov. 12, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said “we want to have a deal that makes sense for them and for us.”

“Part of it means protecting our supply chains and getting them here, but also making accommodation when possible,” Greer said.

Trump said Friday that when Canada’s trade deficit with the United States is down to zero, he’ll be ready to talk. That trade deficit is driven by U.S. consumption of oil and energy products, which Trump also has said he wants to increase.

The president repeated Friday the claim that Carney wants to “build a Keystone pipeline for us” — likely a reference to the Prairie Connector pipeline that would reuse Keystone XL infrastructure.

Carney on Wednesday said a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but Canada won’t just sit around and wait.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026
